papers.title: What Does LALM Post-training Learn? Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
papers.abstract: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: AdaFrame: Hierarchical Multimodal Deduplication with Adaptive Information Budgeting for Cost-Efficient Video Advertisement Analysis
papers.abstract: Uniform frame sampling for vision-language model (VLM)-based video analysis often floods multimodal backbones with redundant content, while existing keyframe selection methods are typically optimized for human viewing rather than downstream extraction accuracy. We propose AdaFrame, a content-adaptive preprocessing cascade that reduces visual redundancy without sacrificing extraction fidelity. Three progressively finer filters, perceptual hashing, learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and CLIP-based semantic clustering, efficiently eliminate redundant frames before costly cross-modal inference. Per-video frame budgets are determined using Intrinsic Semantic Dimensionality (ISD), which estimates each video's semantic complexity through singular value decomposition of its frame embeddings. Experiments on 500 video advertisements from the Pitt Ads Dataset show that AdaFrame reduces the frame count by 48 percent and VLM inference cost by 75 percent compared with uniform sampling, while achieving 86.0 percent topic accuracy, an improvement of 1.6 percentage points, and 79.4 percent sentiment accuracy, an improvement of 7.5 percentage points.

papers.title: Shared Sentiment Evidence from Frozen Multimodal Models for Continuous Sentiment Prediction
papers.abstract: Continuous multimodal sentiment analysis estimates polarity and intensity from linguistic, acoustic, and visual cues that may disagree. Hard judgments compress sentiment alternatives, while learned fusion interfaces tie task adaptation to model representations. We introduce Shared Sentiment Evidence (SSE), an output-space interface with fixed view and sentiment-option semantics across frozen backbones. Four queries yield five-option distributions whose probabilities, entropy, and cross-view relations form a 28-dimensional vector for CatBoost regression. On CH-SIMS-v2 and CMU-MOSI, the Qwen-based interface improves on supervised joint-only readout. Matched Ridge and CatBoost controls assess the contributions of additional views, deterministic summaries, and nonlinear readout. With the same interface specification and fixed readout settings, separately fitted heads also improve on joint-only prediction for three additional frozen backbones. These results support learning continuous sentiment from reusable output coordinates.

papers.title: Lluna: Collaborative Unimodal Models for Missing-Modality Inference
papers.abstract: Pretrained unimodal models offer a flexible route to multimodal prediction through collaboration, but this collaboration can become less accurate than a surviving unimodal model when modalities are missing. We study this setting using fixed surviving-model anchors and find that collaborative gains can weaken or reverse as inputs disappear, even when the anchor's own input is unchanged. Our diagnostics further reveal reduced recovery of modality-specific information after aggregation and state-dependent collaborative representations. We propose Lluna, which combines a direct private prediction path from adapted unimodal features with a common graph-based collaboration branch that provides a residual correction. Progressive Collaboration Consistency organizes richer-to-poorer guidance along single-modality removals, aligning normalized common representations while task supervision adapts predictions to the available evidence. Across eight datasets spanning affective computing, scene understanding, and medical prediction, Lluna achieves the best evaluated average performance over non-full input states, improving Mean-Missing by 4.26\% on average relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. The fixed-anchor diagnostic also shows positive gains in mean collaboration under minimal inputs on all eight tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/AIFrontierLab/Lluna.

papers.title: Frame Rate, Not the Grid: A Confound in Single-Clip Optical ENF Video Forensics
papers.abstract: The optical electric network frequency, the faint mains-driven flicker imprinted on rolling-shutter video, is increasingly proposed for verifying where footage was captured and for flagging manipulated or generated video. This letter shows that reading the mains frequency from a single short clip is confounded by the camera frame rate: at the rates in common use, a harmonic of that rate lands in the same narrow band as the true flicker, so the recovered grid is set by the frame rate, not the supply, and the estimator returns a confident value instead of abstaining. The underlying aliasing is known; its forensic consequence is not, and is the contribution here. On the 804 clips with a measurable in-band line the flicker feature does not separate genuine from generated video (area under the curve 0.509), while the recovered grid tracks the frame rate exactly for the generators, and a controlled synthesis confirms the mechanism against ground truth for genuine grids. Single-clip grid, and hence region, identification is therefore unreliable at the standard rates, and a comb-aware estimator that models the frame-rate harmonics restores the distinction between a genuine grid and a frame-rate comb under controlled conditions.

papers.title: Perceptual Characterization of Scan-induced Artifacts in Dynamic 3D Meshes
papers.abstract: Dynamic meshes reconstructed from real-world scenes often exhibit scan-induced artifacts such as surface jitter and missing geometry, which strongly impact perceived visual quality. Objective assessment remains challenging due to the absence of artifact-free ground truth and limited perceptual understanding of artifact interactions. This paper presents a systematic and controlled perceptual study of scan-induced artifacts in dynamic meshes, focusing on surface jitter and holes. To enable systematic analysis, we introduce a physically grounded artifact synthesis framework in which holes are synthesized using a reconstruction uncertainty model derived from multi-view geometry. The study reveals asymmetric cross-artifact interactions, non-additive integration, and motion-dependent temporal masking. Based on these findings, we propose a compact, perceptually grounded no-reference quality assessment framework that encodes the observed perceptual mechanisms.

papers.title: GenState-AI: State-Aware Dataset for Text-to-Video Retrieval on AI-Generated Videos
papers.abstract: Existing text-to-video retrieval benchmarks often permit matching from static appearance, making it difficult to determine whether models capture state changes and final outcomes. We introduce GenState-AI, a benchmark comprising 956 AI-generated videos and 195 verified state-change queries across Toy, Cartoon, Home, and Manipulation domains. Its construction uses prompt-controlled variants that target either conflicting temporal/state outcomes or semantic substitutions. Following human verification, all valid videos contribute to subset-level retrieval pools, while complete query-specific triplets support diagnostic hard-negative ordering. We evaluate VCF-Lik, Qwen3-VL, and LanguageBind using both standard Recall@K and triplet-based consistency metrics. Qwen3-VL (8B) achieves the best macro-average R@1 and triplet consistency, while LanguageBind obtains the highest semantic discrimination accuracy. However, stronger retrieval does not consistently yield correct hard-negative ordering, and Qwen3-VL and LanguageBind remain weak on Manipulation triplets, where VCF-Lik performs substantially better. GenState-AI therefore provides a controlled diagnostic testbed for distinguishing global retrieval quality from fine-grained temporal and semantic grounding in AI-generated videos.
